doc.title: Earl Watkins interviewed by Monk Rowe, San Francisco, California, August 7, 2002

title: Employment restrictions, Barbary Coast history and segregation
summary: Black bands were shut out east of Divisadero; contrast with the integrated Barbary Coast.

story.theme_name: The musicians' union: cards, locals, and the Black-white merger
story.community_name: The musicians' union: cards, scale and the black-white merger

blocks.x: saying, you had no say and also your employment was restricted. In San Francisco anything east of Divisidero the people wouldn’t hire you. See they wouldn’t hire. The club owners wouldn’t hire, and I told you that story about the Dawn Club and Wilbert Baranco. And now that’s the story that he told me. See he was directly involved. And now there was some isolated incidents, very isolated engagements where black musicians were hired. Eddie Alley, Vernon’s brother, told me a story, he worked at a place on Pacific Avenue and it was gangster owned. And so they told the union, the union reps, “You leave this band alone. I want this band, and this is my club.” So Eddie, he worked down on Pacific Avenue so that had to be in the very early thirties. And of course prior to that, see if you go back into the history about San Francisco and when we had Barbary Coast, the Barbary Coast was integrated. They had colored bands, you had colored entertainers, that was all down on Broadway and Pacific Avenue. There is a book written by a guy Jim Goggin and Sid Laprate is the name of the pianist that is mainly featured. As a matter of fact it’s about Sid’s history. And Sid — oh it’s a marvelous book because it gives you the history going back to the — what do they call it? The Texas trot or something. The different dances that they did and what they used to do in the Barbary Coast and they were all colored bands. Kid Ory was even — he was out here in the early twenties. And I think Hines was out here, oh, he was out here in the twenties, I think the mid-twenties, before he became band leader at the Grand Terrace in Chicago. He was out here. But see but then I don’t know whether it was the depression, but the city, we always had kind of like, there was racial segregation at all times, against the Chinese, against the Japanese, against the colored. Most restaurants wouldn’t serve you. With us, if you wanted to go to a restaurant you went to a Japanese restaurant. If you wanted a hotel room you went to a Japanese hotel. See they would take care of you. And in Chinatown, you’d go there and they’d tell you you have to have a reservation. Unless it was a slow night. If there was nobody in the place then they’d let you in and put you in the corner and put a screen around you.
